blocks.text: 1-year prevalence of depression in the general population is ==5.3%==; lifetime prevalence ==13%==. **NESARC**: mean age of onset 30 years; first episode occurs before age 40 in ~==50%== of patients.
Most common comorbidities: alcohol use (>==40%==) and anxiety (>==40%==); ==30%== have a personality disorder. Suicide is attempted by ==9%== of those with **MDD**.

In ~==56%== of patients the initial diagnosis of depressive disorder changes on follow-up — mainly to schizophrenic spectrum (==16%==), personality disorder (==9%==), neurotic/stress-related/somatoform (==8%==), or bipolar disorder (==8%==) (Kessing, 2005).

blocks.text: Treat comorbid depression before anxiety if both are present. Watchful waiting (review in 2 weeks) for mild depression if agreeable; antidepressants are not advocated for mild depression given a poor risk–benefit ratio there.
"Which comorbidity should be treated first?" → **NICE** explicitly wants comorbid depression treated **BEFORE** anxiety — treating anxiety first is presented as the wrong (non-recommended) answer.

blocks.text: SSRIs are first-line antidepressants. For severe depression at presentation, combine antidepressant + **CBT** (more cost-effective than either alone). Continue antidepressants ≥6 months after remission for a moderate/severe episode; ≥2 years if >2 recent episodes or residual impairment.

**ECT** is reserved for rapid/short-term improvement of severe symptoms after an adequate trial of other treatment has failed, and/or when the condition is potentially life-threatening; **ECT** maintenance is not recommended.

Antidepressant response/remission NNTs (**FDA** reanalysis): adults **NNT** ~4–5 for response, ~6–7 for remission over 12–14-week trials. In the elderly, **NNT** is 4 for tricyclics, 8 for SSRIs, 3 for MAOIs.

Kirsch's meta-analysis (47 **FDA** trials): drug–placebo **HRSD** difference was only 1.80 points overall, below **NICE**'s 3-point clinical-significance threshold — but the effect size grew with baseline severity, exceeding the **NICE**-significant threshold only above an **HRSD** baseline of ~28.

Antidepressants and suicide: **MHRA**/**FDA** black-box warning applies to under-25s (risk neutral 25–64, protective ≥65). **BAP** (2015): **SSRI** treatment is not associated with increased completed suicide in adults and is linked to a small (<==1%==) rise in non-fatal suicidal ideation in adolescents/young adults.

"Do antidepressants increase suicide risk?" — the expected, guideline-backed answer is that suicides occur **MORE** often among those **NOT** on an antidepressant; don't let the black-box-warning framing pull you toward the intuitive-but-wrong answer.

blocks.text: Antidepressant toxicity in overdose (Hawton 2010): TCAs > **venlafaxine**/**mirtazapine** > SSRIs in toxicity. Within TCAs, **dosulepin** and **doxepin** are more toxic than **amitriptyline**; within SSRIs, **citalopram** has the highest case fatality.

Khan, analysing **FDA** data, concluded no increase in adult suicides with antidepressants — but **Healy** reappraised the same data and found ==1.62 times== more suicides, arguing this is a significant difference. This Khan-vs-Healy disagreement over the *same* dataset is a good illustration of how reappraisal can flip a safety conclusion.

From epidemiological/cross-sectional data, it is more likely that **suicidal behaviour leads to treatment** (reverse causality) than treatment causing suicidal behaviour. One finding that doesn't make biological sense is quoted as an illustration: **sertraline appears to increase self-harm but not suicide risk** — a result that doesn't fit a simple causal story, underlining why this evidence base is hard to interpret. The reported association also does **not** appear to be a general psychotropic-prescription effect: prescription-related suicides are **not** seen with **antipsychotic** use (Khan, 2001).

bullets.text: Treat comorbid depression **BEFORE** anxiety; watchful waiting (2wk review) for mild depression — no antidepressants there.
**SSRI** first-line; severe depression → antidepressant + **CBT** combo. Continue ≥6 months post-remission (moderate/severe), ≥2 years if >2 episodes or residual symptoms.
**ECT**: rapid relief of severe/life-threatening depression after treatment failure only; no maintenance **ECT**.
**NNT**: response ~4–5, remission ~6–7 (12–14wk trials). Elderly **NNT**: tricyclics 4, SSRIs 8, MAOIs 3.
Kirsch meta-analysis: drug–placebo **HRSD** gap only 1.80 (below **NICE**'s 3-point threshold), exceeding it only above baseline **HRSD** ~28.

Suicide warning applies to under-25s only (neutral 25–64, protective ≥65); **BAP**: SSRIs not linked to completed suicide in adults, though linked to a small (<==1%==) rise in non-fatal suicidal ideation in adolescents/young adults.

Overdose toxicity: TCAs > **venlafaxine**/**mirtazapine** > SSRIs (Hawton 2010); within TCAs **dosulepin**/**doxepin** more toxic than **amitriptyline**; **citalopram** highest **SSRI** case fatality.
Khan (FDA data): no adult suicide increase. Healy reappraised same data: ==1.62x== more suicides — a genuine analytic disagreement, not just a guideline update.

Reverse-causality caveat: suicidal behaviour likely *leads to* treatment, not the other way round. Sertraline's self-harm-but-not-suicide signal is biologically implausible. Antipsychotics show no equivalent prescription-linked suicide signal.

blocks.text: **STAR*D** (pragmatic **RCT**, n=4041): Level 1 **citalopram**; Level 2 switch (**bupropion** SR/**sertraline**/**venlafaxine** XR) or augment (**bupropion**/**buspirone**) or combine with **CBT**; Level 3 switch to **mirtazapine**/**nortriptyline** or augment with **lithium**/thyroid hormone; Level 4 switch to **tranylcypromine** (**MAOI**) or **venlafaxine**+**mirtazapine** combo. Remission fell and relapse rose at each successive level (==37%==→==31%==→==14%==→==13%== remission). Cumulative remission after all 4 steps: ==67%==.

blocks.text: Combining two antidepressants: evidence base is sparse. **Venlafaxine** + **mirtazapine** ("Californian rocket fuel") has some support in **TRD**. Serotonin syndrome is a particular risk with **SSRI**+**MAOI** combinations. No single combination has proven superior head-to-head.

**STAR*D** methodology: a *pragmatic* **RCT** — nearly ⅔ of participants had a comorbid physical disorder, nearly ⅔ had a comorbid psychiatric diagnosis, and ~==40%== had depression onset before age 18 — deliberately close to real-world presentations. 4041 patients were enrolled across 25 US sites. "Measurement-based care" was used throughout: routine symptom/side-effect measurement at each visit, with a treatment manual guiding dose changes tailored to the individual. Patients tended to choose their next step based on their experience so far — a **partial** response led them to prefer **augmentation**, while **non-response** led them to prefer **switching**.

**STAR*D** drop-out rose across levels: ==21%== withdrew after Level 1, ==30%== withdrew after Level 2, and ==42%== withdrew after Level 3 — the source data does not report a separate Level 4 drop-out figure — on top of the rising intolerance/relapse figures already noted. About half of participants became symptom-free after only **two** treatment levels; the cumulative *non-response* rate after all 4 steps was ==33%== (i.e. the mirror of the ==67%== cumulative remission figure).

Novel antidepressant mechanisms (Palaniyappan & McAllister-Williams, 2007): **agomelatine** is a **5-HT2C antagonist** and melatonergic agonist — 5-HT2C stimulation normally drives GABA interneurons that tonically inhibit noradrenergic/dopaminergic circuits to the prefrontal cortex, so 5-HT2C antagonism *disinhibits* those circuits. Clinical efficacy is confirmed, though how much the melatonergic action itself contributes is unclear.

**Ketamine** acts via glutamatergic **NMDA** receptor blockade with relative **AMPA** receptor upregulation (also implicating **mTOR** and **BDNF** signalling) — an extremely rapidly-acting antidepressant. A single 0.5mg/kg dose showed a large effect vs placebo at 24 hours (effect size ==1.46==, ==71%== response), but the effect decayed to ==0.68== by 1 week, with no pharmacological augmentation yet shown to sustain it.

St John's Wort's (**Hypericum perforatum**) evidence base shrank on reanalysis: an initial 2001 meta-analysis found a relative risk of ==1.94== favouring it, but adding 3 later studies dropped the effect size to ==1.30== — a caution against citing the earlier, larger figure. It can also increase the effect of conventional **SSRIs**.

**Agomelatine** = 5-HT2C antagonist + melatonergic agonist (disinhibits NE/DA circuits). **Ketamine** = NMDA blockade/AMPA upregulation, effect size ==1.46==→==0.68== over 1 week.

blocks.text: **NCS-R** lifetime prevalence: bipolar I ==1.0%==, bipolar **II** ==1.1%==, subsyndromal bipolar spectrum ==2.4%==. Mean age of onset: **BP-I** 18.2 years, **BP-II** ~20 years. Suicide rate in bipolar disorder is 15–18x the general population.

Once diagnosed, bipolar disorder's diagnostic stability is 70–==91%==; bipolar I is more stable than bipolar **II** (**II** can switch to I but not vice versa). **NICE**: recurrence risk after a mood episode is ~==50%== at 1 year and >==70%== at 4 years.

blocks.text: Bipolar **II** patients spend more time depressed than bipolar I (==93%== vs ==67%== of symptomatic time is depressive) — thought to explain higher suicidality/poorer functional recovery in bipolar **II** despite "milder" mania.
Perlis (**STEP-BD**): the single biggest predictor of relapse is residual symptoms, and most relapses are into depression.

Rapid cycling = ≥4 episodes/year; ultra-rapid = ≥4/month; ultradian = switching within a day on ≥4 days/week. ~==20%== of bipolar patients rapid-cycle (**STEP-BD**); ~==80%== of rapid cyclers are women. Current hypothyroidism and poor **lithium** response are associated with rapid cycling.

"Switch" (antidepressant-induced mania, within ~2 months of starting) is distinct from "mood destabilization" (long-term increase in episode frequency from antidepressant use) — a drug can cause one without the other.

blocks.text: **DSM-5** now emphasises changes in activity/energy as well as mood when diagnosing manic and hypomanic episodes.

Prodrome: a predominantly insidious prodrome (>1 year) is seen in more than half of bipolar patients; acute presentations (<1 month prodrome) are rare. Prodrome duration doesn't differ between psychotic and non-psychotic mania. Attenuated positive symptoms and increased goal-directed activity are significantly more common in the prodrome of later psychotic mania specifically. Mania and schizophrenia prodromes overlap considerably, but subsyndromal unusual ideas are more likely part of the schizophrenia prodrome specifically, while obsessions/compulsions, suicidality, difficulty thinking/communicating, depressed mood, decreased concentration/memory, tiredness, mood lability, and physical agitation are more likely part of the mania prodrome.

**Ambelas** confirmed a strong correlation between stressful life events and *first manic* admissions specifically (not depressive ones) — this correlation lessens as illness progresses and is significantly linked to mania, not depression, particularly in younger patients. Sleep reduction may be a final common pathway to mania.

Prodrome >1yr insidious in >half; overlaps with schizophrenia prodrome but unusual ideas favour schizophrenia while mood/energy/cognitive symptoms favour mania. Ambelas: stressful life events correlate specifically with *first manic* (not depressive) admissions.

Predominant polarity (Vieta & Phillips): depressive (~⅓, more in BP2, more seasonal, more suicide attempts, better lamotrigine response) vs manic (~¼, more in BP1, more substance use, better antipsychotic response). ==56%== show a predominant-polarity pattern.

blocks.text: Acute de novo mania: antipsychotic first-line (**haloperidol**, **olanzapine**, **quetiapine** or **risperidone**) for rapid anti-manic effect. Do **NOT** offer **lamotrigine** for mania. If already on an antidepressant, consider stopping it, then offer an antipsychotic regardless.

Bipolar depression: offer a bipolar-specific/high-intensity psychological intervention first-line. If drug-naive with moderate/severe bipolar depression, **NICE** suggests **fluoxetine**+**olanzapine** combination, or **quetiapine** alone. Second step: **lamotrigine**.

Maintenance: **lithium** monotherapy first-line — more effective against mania than depression, and reduces suicide risk. **Valproate** probably prevents both manic and depressive relapse; **olanzapine** prevents manic more than depressive relapse; **lamotrigine** prevents depressive more than manic relapse; **carbamazepine** is less effective than **lithium**.
**Lithium** toxicity with neurological symptoms → haemodialysis is the expected answer once levels exceed the life-threatening 2.0 mmol/L threshold, not simply stopping the drug.

blocks.text: **NICE** maintenance duration: continue ≥2 years after an episode, up to 5 years if high relapse-risk factors are present.
Mixed episodes: treat as manic episodes, avoid antidepressants; best evidence is for **valproate** (more effective than **lithium**/placebo).

Bauer's definition: a true "mood stabiliser" must show efficacy in all four of acute mania, acute depression, manic prophylaxis, and depressive prophylaxis — by that strict definition, only **lithium** qualifies.

**Antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria**: a distinct phenomenon in some bipolar patients on long-term antidepressants — possibly the bipolar equivalent of antidepressant "tachyphylaxis"/poop-out seen in unipolar depression. A triad of irritability, middle insomnia (restless sleep/night-time waking), and dysphoria is typical. Discontinuing the antidepressant usually resolves these symptoms slowly, without worsening the underlying depressive symptoms (El-Mallakh & Karippot, 2006). Tricyclic antidepressants carry a greater switch-to-mania risk than other antidepressant classes; because bipolar depressive episodes tend to be shorter than unipolar ones, antidepressants may be discontinued after 3–4 months.

**Vigabatrin** has no proven efficacy in bipolar disorder and is associated with visual field defects (and can cause psychosis) as a side effect. **Topiramate** and **phenytoin** similarly have no place in bipolar treatment — don't mistake "is an anticonvulsant" for "has mood-stabilising evidence".
**CBT** for bipolar disorder includes: psychoeducation, self-monitoring, self-regulation (action plans and behaviour modification), and increased treatment compliance.

**NICE** recognises bipolar disorder as possible in those under 18 and encourages use of adult diagnostic criteria, with three exceptions: (1) mania must be present for a **BPAD** diagnosis; (2) euphoria must be present most days, most of the time, for 7 days; (3) irritability is not a core diagnostic criterion on its own, but can be helpful in adolescents if it is episodic, severe, impairs function, and is out of character for the individual.

bullets.text: Acute mania: antipsychotic first-line (**haloperidol**/**olanzapine**/**quetiapine**/**risperidone**); NEVER **lamotrigine** for mania; stop antidepressant + start antipsychotic regardless.
Bipolar depression: psychological intervention first-line; drug-naive moderate/severe → **fluoxetine**+**olanzapine** or **quetiapine** alone; 2nd step **lamotrigine**.
Maintenance: **lithium** first-line (best for mania, ↓suicide risk); **valproate** both phases; **olanzapine** > mania; **lamotrigine** > depression; **carbamazepine** < **lithium**.
Maintenance duration: ≥2yr post-episode, up to 5yr if high relapse risk.
Mixed episodes: treat as mania, avoid antidepressants; **valproate** has best evidence.
Bauer's strict 'mood stabiliser' definition (efficacy in all 4: acute mania, acute depression, manic & depressive prophylaxis) — only **lithium** qualifies.

Antidepressant-associated chronic irritable dysphoria: irritability + middle insomnia + dysphoria triad, resolves slowly on stopping the antidepressant (El-Mallakh & Karippot 2006). TCAs = highest switch-to-mania risk; bipolar depressive episodes shorter than unipolar → can stop antidepressant at 3–4 months.
**Vigabatrin**/**topiramate**/**phenytoin**: no proven bipolar efficacy despite being anticonvulsants; vigabatrin also risks visual field defects/psychosis.
**NICE** paediatric BPAD: adult criteria apply except mania must be present, euphoria most days for 7 days, and irritability alone only counts if episodic/severe/impairing/out-of-character.

blocks.text: Perinatal complications: low birth weight was initially implicated as a schizophrenia risk factor, then anoxic brain damage at delivery (hypoxia dose correlated with neuronal death). **Kendell (1996)** found pregnancy-induced hypertension increased psychosis risk almost **9-fold** in a retrospective study. Three obstetric-event types are described: growth-related (low birth weight, small for gestational age), perinatal (PIH), and hypoxic (premature rupture of membranes). The **Lewis-Murray scale** measures obstetric complications during childbirth, though odds ratios across studies have been too low to reach significance.

Cannabis (expanding on the pooled **OR** 2.1 already noted): confounders like amphetamine use don't explain the association alone, and reverse causality remains plausible but unproven. In the **Dunedin cohort**, cannabis exposure at age 15 predicted psychosis at age 26 even after adjusting for psychotic liability at age 11. A **Greek cohort study** tested the self-medication hypothesis by comparing cannabis associations with distressing vs non-distressing subtle psychotic experiences — associations were *stronger* with non-distressing experiences, making self-medication theory unlikely (though a bidirectional association remains possible). Cannabis shows a dose-response relationship to psychosis outcome, with exposure typically preceding the outcome and plausible biological mechanisms via endocannabinoid neurodevelopmental effects or dopamine sensitisation.

blocks.text: **Clozapine** is the only drug showing moderate-to-large effect-size superiority over FGAs (in resistant illness, not first-episode). **CATIE** and **CUtLASS** found SGAs no better than FGAs on efficacy/cost overall.

No **RCT** evidence for a first-generation "correct" mean dose, but there is for SGAs. Near-maximal effective doses: **haloperidol** 3.3–10mg/day; **aripiprazole** 10mg/day; **olanzapine** possibly >16mg/day; **risperidone** 4mg/day (2mg gives lower efficacy; ≥10mg no added benefit, more **EPSE**).

blocks.text: **NICE** for a first episode: oral atypical first-line; **clozapine** at the earliest sign of treatment resistance; do not routinely switch a well-controlled patient on a typical to an atypical; atypicals and typicals should not be co-prescribed except briefly during a changeover.
Maintenance: ~==20%== relapse within a year on treatment vs ~==60%== off it; stopping medication raises relapse risk ~5-fold. Multi-episode patients: maintenance for ≥5 years, possibly indefinite.

Depot myths (Maudsley): **NMS** risk is not higher for depot vs oral; **NMS** history is not a depot contraindication; tardive dyskinesia risk is not higher for depot vs oral of the same drug; many patients on depot prefer it once tried.

Depot myths: **NMS** risk/history and tardive dyskinesia risk are **NOT** higher for depot vs oral of the same drug.
High-dose (>1g **chlorpromazine**-equivalent): avoid; no evidence in non-responders; increase no more than weekly; **ECG** monitoring; stop after 3 months if no response.

blocks.text: **NICE** treatment-resistance definition: lack of satisfactory response to sequential adequate (6–8 week) trials of ≥2 antipsychotics, at least one being a non-**clozapine** atypical.

Kane et al. (1988): **clozapine** ==30%== responders vs **chlorpromazine** ==4%== in treatment-resistant illness. Meltzer: ~==30%== respond by 6 weeks, a further ==20%== by 3 months, 10–==20%== more by 6 months — trial **clozapine** monotherapy for at least 6 months. Plasma level ~350–450 ng/mL is the usual non-response threshold.
Best evidence for suicide-risk reduction in schizophrenia is **clozapine** (**InterSePT** trial vs **olanzapine**) — a very frequently tested factual pairing.

In the **clozapine**-vs-other-**SGA** phase, **clozapine** had the lowest discontinuation, ~3x longer time-to-discontinuation.
**CATIE**'s first-generation comparator drug was **perphenazine** specifically (not **haloperidol**) — a commonly misremembered detail.

blocks.text: **CUtLASS**: unblinded **RCT**, no advantage of SGAs over FGAs for quality of life/symptoms at 1 year (**FGA** group did relatively better). **CUtLASS** 2: **clozapine** showed significant symptom advantage over other SGAs in non-responders, and patients preferred it.

blocks.title: CATIE controversies

items.text: A complicated study design generated many different analysable outcomes from one dataset.
**Ziprasidone** was added to the protocol only after recruitment had already begun.
**Perphenazine** (the first-generation comparator) was used in only one randomised phase (phase 1) of the study.
Using double-blinded treatment reduced how closely the study resembled routine clinical care.
The mean doses used remain controversial, despite the trial's pragmatic (not purely experimental) design intent.

blocks.text: **CUtLASS** enrolled ==1227== patients being reviewed for poor response/adverse effects; second-generation drugs used were amisulpride, olanzapine, quetiapine or risperidone; follow-up rate was ==81%== at 1 year. Participants reported **no clear preference** for either drug class overall (contrast with **CUtLASS 2**, where patients did prefer **clozapine**).

**Deficit schizophrenia** (primary, enduring negative symptoms) full diagnostic definition: (1) at least 2 of 6 clinically-significant features — restricted affect, diminished emotional range, poverty of speech, curbing of interest, diminished sense of purpose, diminished social drive; (2) present for the preceding 12 months and always present during periods of clinical stability; (3) idiopathic — not secondary to anxiety, drug effects/EPSE, suspiciousness, formal thought disorder, hallucinations/delusions, intellectual disability, or depression; (4) meets **DSM-5** schizophrenia criteria. Deficit-form prevalence: ==20–30%== of clinical samples, ==14–17%== of population/incidence samples.

blocks.title: Deficit syndrome associations

blocks.text: Deficit schizophrenia is associated with **poorer** functional outcome overall, but paradoxically **lower** suicide and depression rates — a counterintuitive pairing worth remembering as its own trap.

Treatment of related psychotic presentations — **delusional disorder**: a triple-blind RCT of fluoxetine in body dysmorphic disorder (==40%== of participants had *delusional* BDD) titrated to a maximum 80mg/day; delusional patients responded to fluoxetine just as well as non-delusional patients (30% BDD-Y-BOCS reduction: ==53%== fluoxetine vs ==18%== placebo, **NNT** 3). No RCTs exist for primary delusional parasitosis — only heterogeneous case reports, with no evidence-based recommendation possible.

**Post-schizophrenic depression**: Levinson's systematic review found antidepressants beneficial once patients are stable with respect to psychotic symptoms, whereas antipsychotics are more effective for depressive symptoms occurring during acute psychosis. Both **clozapine** (vs olanzapine) and **olanzapine** (vs haloperidol) show antisuicidal effects in schizophrenia.

**Schizoaffective disorder**: mood stabilisers are the mainstay of treatment. **Carbamazepine is specifically superior for the depressive subtype**; lithium and carbamazepine show no efficacy difference for the manic (bipolar-like) subtype. Antidepressant treatment follows the same approach as bipolar depression.

blocks.text: Despite overall high withdrawal rates in the psychotic-depression trials, there was no significant difference in withdrawal *between* treatments. Both the **APA** and **NICE** recommend antidepressant+antipsychotic combination as first-line for psychotic depression.

blocks.title: Relapse within 1 year — antipsychotics vs placebo

blocks.text: High expressed emotion (Brown & Rutter) raises relapse risk despite adequate pharmacotherapy; family therapy cuts relapse from ~==64%== to ~==24%== in such families (Cochrane **NNT** ~6, Pharaoh 2000).

Long-term outcome studies (Iowa 500, Bonn, Chestnut Lodge, Vermont, **WHO** ISoS/DOSMeD) consistently show a more favourable long-term course than clinicians typically assume, and better outcomes in developing countries than developed ones.

High-risk prediction studies: individuals at enhanced genetic risk (family history) are thought to inherit a state of vulnerability with transient/partial psychosis-like symptoms, though not all develop florid schizophrenia. **Edinburgh High Risk Study** (Johnstone et al., 2005): the 10% risk in those with high-risk family history rises to nearly 50% in the subgroup with high schizotypal-cognition and social-withdrawal scores; episodic-memory measures significantly discriminate converters (suggestive of temporal lobe dysfunction, though whether temporal lobe volume deteriorates over time remains controversial).

**Australian PACE clinic**: 20 of 49 ultra-high-risk subjects (==40.8%==) developed a psychotic disorder within 12 months; significant predictors were long prodrome duration, poor functioning at intake, low-grade psychotic symptoms, depression, and disorganisation. **German Bonn Basic Symptoms** criteria study: very high conversion rate in help-seeking individuals over ~10 years; of the Bonn Scale's 5 symptom clusters, thought/language/perception/motor disturbances showed significantly greater predictive discrimination than any other cluster. **NAPLS** (North American Prodrome Longitudinal Study): ultra-high-risk (UHR) criteria predict early transition to psychosis with a relative risk of ==405== vs general-population incidence; predictive power is enhanced by genetic risk, functional impairment, and higher baseline psychopathology (especially odd beliefs/suspiciousness) — substance use (not a specific class) also raises predictive value, and the three variables together roughly double predictive power.

Psychoeducation (Bauml et al.): psychosocial interventions in schizophrenia are classified as **obligatory** (psychoeducation — empowering patients/relatives to understand and cope with the illness) vs **voluntary** (individual behavioural therapy, self-assertiveness training, problem-solving training, communication training, further family therapy). The term "psychoeducation" was first used by **Anderson**, describing a 4-element behavioural-therapeutic concept: briefing on the illness, problem-solving training, communication training, and self-assertiveness training, with relatives included. Cochrane review: reduces relapse, improves compliance, does not increase suicidal thoughts.

**Social skills training** (Bellack & Mueser framework) has three models: (1) **basic model** — complex social repertoires broken into simpler steps via corrective learning/role-play, applied in natural settings; (2) **social problem-solving model** — targets information-processing impairments across medication/symptom management, recreation, conversation, self-care; (3) **cognitive remediation model** — targets fundamental cognitive impairments (attention, planning) on the assumption that improvement transfers to more complex processes.

**CBT for psychosis** (Turkington's elements): (1) therapeutic alliance — validation without colluding with delusions; (2) improving medication adherence; (3) alternate explanations for unusual experiences (normalisation); (4) decreasing the impact of positive symptoms (e.g. addressing the omnipotence of voices); (5) graded reality testing via peripheral questioning and inference chaining. A meta-analysis of 34 trials found beneficial effects on target symptom (effect size ==0.4==), positive symptoms, negative symptoms, functioning, mood, and social anxiety (effects ==0.35–0.44==) — but no effect on hopelessness. Trials with unblinded raters showed inflated effect sizes (==50–100%== larger).

**Vocational rehabilitation**: competitive employment is estimated at <==20%== for severely mentally ill persons, likely lower in schizophrenia specifically. Supported-employment programmes use an individual "place-and-train" model (vs traditional train-and-place) with 6 common components: permanent competitive-employment goal, minimal employability screening, avoidance of preoccupational training, individualised placement, time-unlimited support, and consideration of client preference. RCT evidence: ==65%== obtained competitive employment on supported-employment programmes vs ==26%== on control interventions.

blocks.text: Suicide: Palmer et al.'s meta-analysis of 61 studies estimated lifetime suicide prevalence in schizophrenia (from first admission/illness onset) at ==5.6%== (95% CI 3.7–8.5%), with most suicides occurring within a few years of onset. Non-fatal self-harm: ==38%== of people with chronic schizophrenia had at least one episode over a 2–12 year follow-up.

Mortality: median standardised mortality rate (**SMR**) for schizophrenia is ==2.58== (no obvious sex difference); suicide carries the highest individual **SMR** (==12.86==), though most major causes of death are elevated. All-cause **SMR** has *increased* over recent decades even though case-fatality rates haven't changed and general-population mortality has fallen — the mortality gap between schizophrenia and the general population has widened over time. **SMRs did not differ by economic status.**

blocks.text: National Psychiatric Morbidity Survey (**NPMS**, 1995): ==15%== of **UK** adults have broadly-defined neurosis at any time, and anxiety disorders are more prevalent than depression — consistent with **US** **ECA**/**NCS** data. But the *most common individual* anxiety diagnosis differs by study: phobic disorder tops **ECA**/**NCS**, while **NPMS** found mixed anxiety-depression (followed by **GAD**) most common in the **UK**. ==25%== of all **GP** consultations are for anxiety-related symptoms.

Mean age of onset by disorder: social phobia ~15y, **OCD** ~20y, panic disorder ~22–25y, **GAD** ~30y; specific phobia varies by subtype — blood/injection/injury and environmental types begin age 5–9y, situational type ~20y. Each successive generation is diagnosed with anxiety disorders at a younger age than the last.

Blood-injection-injury phobia: lifetime prevalence ~==3.5%==, median onset age 5–6y; strongly associated with a personal history of fainting/seizures. Prevalence is lower in the elderly and higher in females and those with less education.

All anxiety disorders are commoner in women — **except** **OCD** (more boys than girls in childhood, equal in adult men and women) and social-phobia **treatment-seeking** specifically (men outnumber women in attending healthcare for social phobia, even though social phobia itself is still more prevalent in women overall).

blocks.text: Acute stress reaction: immediate, clear temporal link to an exceptional stressor; symptoms usually resolve within 2–3 days (often hours); a mixed, changing symptom picture (numbness, depression, anxiety, anger, overactivity, withdrawal) rather than one dominant symptom.

**DSM-5** reclassified **PTSD** (and acute stress disorder) out of anxiety disorders into a new **"trauma and stressor-related disorders"** class. Diagnosis requires exposure to a qualifying traumatic event plus symptoms from **four** clusters: intrusion, avoidance, negative alterations in cognition/mood (including persistent self-blame or blaming others), and alterations in arousal/reactivity (including reckless/destructive behaviour). A **"with dissociative symptoms"** subtype was also added.

blocks.text: Eye Movement Desensitisation and Reprocessing (**EMDR**) was discovered serendipitously by psychologist Francine Shapiro, who first applied it to herself. Its proposed mechanism: bilateral stimulation (typically eye movements) while focusing on traumatic images/cognitions allows reprocessing of traumatic memories. A meta-analysis (Bisson et al., 2007) found no difference in efficacy between trauma-focused **CBT** and **EMDR**, though both were superior to stress management and other therapies.
Outcome: more than **one-third** of people with **PTSD** still had the disorder ==6 years== after onset; there is a ==50%== chance of remission at ==2 years==.

Acute stress reaction should **not** be diagnosed as a sudden exacerbation of an already-diagnosed psychiatric disorder — the one exception is personality disorder (**ICD-10 F60**), where a superimposed acute stress reaction can still be diagnosed.

blocks.text: Evidence review (Ernst, Advances in Psychiatric Treatment 2007): **kava** (*Piper methysticum*) has trial evidence for anxiolysis; ginkgo and valerian are not effective; common lavender, saffron, German chamomile and lemon balm appear promising but are less well studied.

Kava's proposed mechanism: kavapyrones act (in animal models) as muscle relaxants/anticonvulsants, protect against strychnine poisoning and reduce limbic excitability — via inhibition of voltage-dependent sodium channels, increased **GABA-A** receptor density, blocked noradrenaline reuptake, and suppressed glutamate release.

A Cochrane review of 11 RCTs found **kava is the only herbal remedy proven effective for anxiety** — but it cannot be recommended clinically: it is associated with (sometimes fatal) hepatotoxicity and has been **withdrawn from the UK market**. Valerian and passiflora showed no efficacy vs diazepam in separate Cochrane reviews.

bullets.text: **Kava** = only herbal remedy with proven anxiolytic efficacy (Cochrane) but **UK**-withdrawn for hepatotoxicity. Ginkgo/valerian not effective.

Interactions: kava+levodopa/alprazolam→EPSE/lethargy; valerian+loperamide/fluoxetine→delirium; evening primrose oil+phenothiazines→seizures.

sections.title: 15. Other Related Disorders (Hypochondriasis, BDD, MUS, Dissociative Disorders)

blocks.text: **Hypochondriasis** (**ICD-10**): preoccupation with fear of serious disease based on misinterpretation of bodily symptoms. **DSM-5** removed the diagnosis (the name was seen as pejorative) — patients would now be diagnosed with **Somatic Symptom Disorder** or **Illness Anxiety Disorder**. Prevalence ==0.8–4.5%== (mostly primary-care data); no clear specific risk factors, but associated with anxiety, depressive and other somatoform disorders. **CBT** (including group **CBT**) and **SSRIs** are efficacious.

**Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD)**: conviction that a body part is defective/flawed despite normal or near-normal appearance, with repetitive behaviours/mental acts about the perceived flaw. **DSM-5** treats psychotic and non-psychotic **BDD** as **one spectrum disorder** (distinguished by degree of insight), not as separate diagnoses.

blocks.title: BDD — predisposing factors, comorbidity and prevalence
rows: Low self-esteem, critical parents/significant others, early childhood trauma, unconscious displacement of emotional conflict
Major depression ==26%== (also earlier depression onset), social phobia ==16%==, OCD ==6%==; higher rates of psychotic disorder and family substance-use disorders

blocks.text: **BDD** treatment: high-dose **SSRIs** for longer than a standard antidepressant trial (fluoxetine has RCT evidence); antipsychotics show variable success; pimozide has anecdotal support but **QT**-prolongation risk limits use; **CBT** effective in case series, ± fluoxetine for resistant cases. Prognosis of the psychotic variant is generally poor (waxing/waning course) but psychosocial function is often relatively preserved — consistent with outcomes in persistent delusional disorder.

**Medically Unexplained Symptoms (MUS) / Somatisation Disorder**: community-survey prevalence <==1%==, but primary-care structured-interview prevalence ==1–2%== — and **WHO** multicentre follow-up data suggest structured-interview recall likely *underestimates* true lifetime prevalence. Prevalence is twice as high in women as men (also true for persistent pain syndromes, seen in ~20% of primary care patients).

Rohricht & Elanjithara (2009): of patients with **MUS**, ==42%== had a primary somatoform diagnosis and ==36%== had a depressive disorder. Sumathipala et al.'s evidence review found three evidence-supported intervention types for **MUS** — antidepressants, **CBT** (strongest, level-I evidence), and other non-specific interventions; no trials have directly compared pharmacological vs psychological treatment, and most only assessed short-term outcomes. Collaborative care models are recommended; body-oriented psychological therapy, mentalisation-based **CBT** and brief psychodynamic interpersonal therapy may also help.

**Dissociative Disorders**: **ICD-10** classifies Conversion Disorder as a dissociative disorder; **DSM-5** lists Dissociative Identity Disorder, Dissociative Amnesia (with Dissociative Fugue as a subtype — reversible amnesia for identity with unplanned travel, sometimes a new identity), and Depersonalisation/Derealisation Disorder.

Dissociative disorder prevalence is estimated at ==10%== of the adult population (**DSM-III**-era definition) — comparable to anxiety, mood and substance-use disorders. Most studies find **no gender difference** in prevalence, though some report more severe presentations in women. High rates of childhood trauma are reported: sexual abuse ==57–90%==, physical abuse 62–82%, emotional abuse 57%, neglect 62%. Treatment aims to integrate feelings/perceptions/thoughts/memories — individual psychotherapy (structured therapies including **ACT** and **DBT**) plus skills training, though the evidence base is still immature.

bullets.text: Hypochondriasis: **DSM-5** removed it → **Somatic Symptom Disorder**/**Illness Anxiety Disorder**. Prevalence ==0.8–4.5%==; **CBT**/**SSRIs** effective.

**BDD**: psychotic/non-psychotic = **one** spectrum (not separate dx); comorbid depression ==26%==, social phobia ==16%==, **OCD** ==6%==; ==7–15%== of cosmetic-surgery, ==12%== of dermatology attenders.
**MUS**: community <==1%== vs primary-care structured-interview ==1–2%== (likely still an underestimate per **WHO** data); **CBT** has strongest evidence.
Dissociative disorders ~==10%== prevalence; childhood sexual abuse in ==57–90%== of cases; no consistent gender difference.

blocks.text: **DSM-5** dropped the amenorrhoea criterion for anorexia — amenorrhoeic and menstruating patients with the same **BMI**/body-image disturbance have similar clinical features and outcome.
Heritability: anorexia nervosa **MZ** ==55%== vs **DZ** ==5%== (significant heritable component); bulimia nervosa **MZ** ==35%== vs **DZ** ==30%== (heritability not significant).

Bradycardia (**HR** ~40 common), orthostatic hypotension and **QT** prolongation are the classic cardiac findings in anorexia; hypercarotenaemia, lanugo hair, Russell's sign (knuckle calluses from induced vomiting) and perimylolysis (dental erosion) are classic physical signs.

Bulimia is **NOT** associated with peptic ulcer — oesophageal tears, dental erosion, seizures (electrolyte-related) and parotid enlargement are the tested complications; peptic ulcer is the deliberate distractor.

blocks.text: **NICE**: drugs must not be sole/primary treatment for anorexia. For bulimia, evidence-based self-help is first-line; **fluoxetine** is first-choice drug at a higher-than-antidepressant dose (60mg/day); **CBT** 16–20 sessions over 4–5 months.

**ICD-10** recognises 3 major eating-disorder types: anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and **EDNOS** (eating disorder not otherwise specified/atypical). Binge eating disorder (**BED**) is increasingly recognised as a 4th type but currently falls under **EDNOS**. Diagnostic stability between categories is poor: ¼ to ⅓ of bulimia patients have a *past* anorexia history, though migration from bulimia to anorexia is rare.
Binge-eating episodes involve food intake of ==1000–2000 kCal==; **DSM-5** requires a once-weekly frequency of binge eating plus compensatory behaviour for a bulimia diagnosis.

Family history of obesity or alcoholism, past history of obesity, early menarche

Adverse parenting (low contact, high expectations, discord), childhood sexual abuse, critical comments about eating/shape/weight, occupational/recreational pressure to be slim, low self-esteem, perfectionism (more in anorexia)

blocks.text: Binge Eating Disorder (**BED**): recurrent bingeing without extreme weight-control behaviours, often against a background of general overeating; associated with obesity (5–10% of obesity-treatment attenders have **BED**). Typical onset in the ==40s==; ==25%== of the **BED** population is male (a higher male proportion than other eating disorders, though still female-predominant overall). High rate of spontaneous remission. Self-help, behavioural weight-loss programmes and **CBT**/**IPT** can help.

blocks.title: Physical signs and investigation findings in eating disorders, by system
rows: Low LH/FSH/oestradiol; low T3 and low-normal T4 with normal TSH ("low T3 syndrome"); mildly raised cortisol; raised growth hormone; low leptin; rare severe hypoglycaemia

Bradycardia (~40 bpm common), orthostatic hypotension, QT-interval prolongation, arrhythmias; ipecac (emetine) can cause reversible myopathy or fatal cardiomyopathy; systolic BP may fall to ~70 in extreme starvation
Delayed gastric emptying, decreased colonic motility (chronic laxative misuse), acute gastric dilatation (rare, from bingeing/re-feeding)
Moderate normocytic normochromic anaemia, mild leucopenia with relative lymphocytosis, thrombocytopenia

Hypercholesterolaemia, raised serum carotene, hypophosphataemia (exaggerated on refeeding), dehydration; vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis + hypokalaemia; laxative misuse causes metabolic acidosis + hyponatraemia + hypokalaemia
Osteopenia/osteoporosis (raised fracture risk); enlarged cerebral ventricles/CSF spaces ("pseudoatrophy")

blocks.text: Eating disorders in pregnancy: reduced fertility (regained near-normal after full recovery); higher rates of hyperemesis gravidarum, anaemia, impaired maternal weight gain, intrauterine growth restriction, prematurity and caesarean delivery, and higher postpartum depression risk. Neonates may show low birth weight, microcephaly, low Apgar scores, and — in actively anorexic mothers — hypoglycaemia.

blocks.text: Bulimia management: **CBT** is most effective (~20 individual sessions over 5 months; ==33–50%== achieve complete, lasting recovery). Antidepressants have a rapid antibulimic effect (reduced bingeing/purging, improved mood) but are less effective than **CBT** and the effect is often not sustained. Anorexia's four therapeutic goals: engagement, weight restoration, psychological therapy (cognitive restructuring), and use of compulsion if needed. Best outpatient prognosis for anorexia: illness present <6 months, no bingeing/vomiting, and cooperative parents willing to engage in family therapy.

Heritability: anorexia **MZ** ==55%== vs **DZ** ==5%== (significant); bulimia **MZ** ==35%== vs **DZ** ==30%== (not significant).
Anorexia: bradycardia (~40), orthostatic hypotension, **QT** prolongation, lanugo, Russell's sign, perimylolysis.
**NICE**: drugs never sole/primary treatment for anorexia; bulimia — self-help first-line, **fluoxetine** 60mg/day, **CBT** 16–20 sessions.
**ICD-10**: anorexia/bulimia/**EDNOS** (3 types); **BED** = emerging 4th, currently under **EDNOS**. ¼–⅓ of bulimia patients have a past anorexia history.

**BED**: ==40s== onset, ==25%== male, high spontaneous remission.
Management evidence: **CBT** strong for bulimia, modest for anorexia; antidepressants considerable (acute) for bulimia only; family therapy for adolescent anorexia.
Bulimia: ~20 **CBT** sessions/5 months, ==33–50%== full recovery. Anorexia: engagement → weight restoration → cognitive restructuring → compulsion if needed.

blocks.text: 5–==13%== of the general population has ≥1 personality disorder; borderline **PD** is generally the most prevalent in psychiatric settings; antisocial (dissocial) **PD** is the most prevalent category in prison settings (==63%== of male remand prisoners in a England & Wales survey).

blocks.text: **NICE**: pharmacological treatment is not recommended for personality disorder features themselves, only for comorbid illness (e.g. depression, **OCD**). Suggested symptom-targeted off-label use: antipsychotics for cognitive/perceptual symptoms, SSRIs for affective dysregulation, mood stabilisers/SSRIs for impulsive-behavioural dyscontrol.

blocks.text: Avoidant **PD** has the *highest* individual-PD prevalence in the Zimmerman psychiatric-outpatient data (==147/1000==) — higher than borderline (==93/1000==). The cluster-level summary (Cluster C > Cluster B overall) hides this individual-PD detail, which is a common exam trap.

blocks.text: General-population **ASPD** prevalence in Great Britain ~==0.6%==; men (==1%==) outnumber women (==0.2%==) 5-fold. International surveys report **ASPD** prevalence ranging ==0.2–4.1%==; higher rates are generally found in urban populations.

McLean Study of Adult Development — borderline symptoms that **decline fastest**: quasi-psychotic thought, self-mutilation, help-seeking suicide efforts, treatment regressions, countertransference problems. Symptoms that **remain common even at 10 years**: chronic dysphoria, intense anger, nondelusional paranoia, and general impulsivity (disordered eating, spending sprees, reckless driving). (Collaborative Longitudinal Personality Disorders Study: abandonment fears and physically self-destructive acts were the *least* stable, remitting fastest.)

Seivewright & Tyrer's 12-year follow-up found personality traits change in **opposite directions by cluster**: Cluster B (antisocial, histrionic) traits became *less* pronounced over time, while Cluster A (schizoid, schizotypal, paranoid) and Cluster C (obsessional, avoidant) traits became *more* pronounced. A common exam trap assumes all personality pathology softens with age.

blocks.text: **"Quasi-psychotic"** is technically an **ICD-10** term specifically for **schizotypal disorder** ("occasional transient quasipsychotic episodes with intense illusions, hallucinations and delusion-like ideas, usually without external provocation") — even though transient stress-induced paranoid ideation in borderline PD is sometimes loosely called this too. Exam questions may test the precise term-to-disorder mapping.

"Quasi-psychotic" is technically an **ICD-10 schizotypal** term, not a borderline one.

blocks.text: Sexual dysfunctions are coded in the **F50** group in **ICD-10**. Classification (DSM-style): sexual desire disorders (sexual aversion, hypoactive sexual desire), sexual arousal disorders (female sexual arousal disorder, male erectile disorder), orgasmic disorders (female/male orgasmic disorder, premature ejaculation), and sexual pain disorders (dyspareunia, vaginismus).

**Hypoactive sexual desire** is the most common — and hardest to treat — female sexual dysfunction. Testosterone has been trialled in both sexes but with only modest effect, largely limited by side effects.

Choosing to undergo humiliation, bondage or suffering for sexual arousal
Choosing to inflict humiliation, bondage or suffering on a partner for sexual arousal
Using objects or non-genital body parts to achieve arousal

blocks.text: '**Other specified paraphilic disorder**' covers rarer paraphilias: zoophilia (animals), scatalogia (obscene phone calls), necrophilia (corpses), coprophilia (faeces), klismaphilia (enemas), and urophilia (urine).

bullets.text: Sexual dysfunctions = **ICD-10 F50**: desire, arousal, orgasmic, pain disorders. Hypoactive sexual desire = commonest & hardest-to-treat female dysfunction.

**DSM-5** paraphilic disorders: voyeurism, exhibitionism, frotteurism, sexual masochism/sadism, paedophilia, fetishism, transvestic disorder + 'other specified' (zoophilia, scatalogia, necrophilia, coprophilia, klismaphilia, urophilia).
